title: The demonic (16.6–16.20)
hook: the Gita's portrait of the other inheritance sounds uncomfortably modern

segments.voice: Yesterday, abhaya: twenty-six divine qualities, starting with fearlessness and purity of heart. Today, the other list.

Hear the word demonic and you probably picture horns, fire, a horror movie. The Gita's picture is quieter, and more unsettling. It's a person lying awake at night, running the numbers. I got this today. Tomorrow I'll get that. This is mine, and that will be mine too. I beat that rival, and I'll beat the others. Who is like me? It sounds less like a monster and more like a very busy, very anxious person. Maybe someone most of us have been, for an evening or two.
screen: `NOT HORNS AND FIRE.` → `SOMEONE AWAKE, RUNNING THE NUMBERS.` → `WHO IS LIKE ME?`

segments.voice: Verse six: there are two kinds of beings in this world, the divine and the asuric, usually translated demonic. In Hindu stories the asuras are the gods' rivals, powerful and proud. Here the word describes a way of living. Verses seven and eight: such people don't know when to act and when to hold back. They say the world has no truth, no ground, no God, and runs on desire alone. Verse ten: gripped by desire that can never be filled, full of hypocrisy, pride and arrogance. Then verses twelve to fifteen, the monologue from the hook. Bound by hundreds of hopes, they pile up wealth by any means. This I gained today, this wish I'll fulfill. I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, strong and happy. Who else is like me? Even their rituals and their giving, verse seventeen says, are done for show, sacrifice in name only. The Gita's verdict is severe: this road leads downward, again and again. Many teachers, especially modern ones, read this chapter less as a label for other people and more as a mirror, though some classical commentators read it as a portrait of a kind of soul. Then verse twenty-one names where it all starts: three gates to hell that destroy the self. Kama, desire; krodha, anger; and lobha, greed. Shut those three, the Gita says, and a person begins to walk toward the highest. The gates aren't beliefs or groups of people. They're three movements inside anyone.
screen: `TWO KINDS OF BEINGS.` · `THIS IS MINE. WHO IS LIKE ME?` · `A MIRROR, NOT A LABEL.` · `DESIRE, ANGER, GREED.` · then, large: `THE DEMONIC.`

segments.voice: Listen for the monologue: something to get, someone to beat, something that's mine. Don't argue with it; just hear it, the way you'd hear a radio in another room. Then check the three gates, desire pulling, anger simmering, a grasping for more, and wherever one is open, breathe out slowly and let it close a little.
The demonic. Gita sixteen: the asuric way of living, restless, proud and grasping, and the three gates that lead there: desire, anger and greed.
Your line: the three gates of hell. Desire, anger, greed. Two hundred fourteen days in.

screen: `DAY 214 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FOLLOW THE SCRIPTURE, NOT DESIRE.`

howItsDone: Hindu teachers often read Gita 16 as a mirror for self-examination rather than a way to label others; the three gates of 16.21, kama, krodha and lobha (desire, anger, greed), are widely quoted.

chat.says: When the Gita says demonic, does it mean actual monsters with horns?
options: No. It describes a way of living: grasping, proud and run by desire.
Yes. It means evil spirits who attack people who skip their prayers.
No. It's a label for other groups who don't share Hindu beliefs.
chat.meaning: Here the word describes a way of living. Its three gates, desire, anger and greed, aren't groups of people; they're movements inside anyone.
